title: n8n Advanced: Self-Hosting, Environments, and Queue Mode Scaling
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# n8n Advanced: Self-Hosting, Environments, and Queue Mode Scaling ##### The instance that fell over at 200 concurrent webhooks A team self-hosted n8n on a 2 GB VPS with the default SQLite database. It handled their 300 daily executions comfortably for eight months. Then a client integration went live and pushed a burst of roughly 200 webhooks in ninety seconds. The n8n process, executing everything in-line in its main event loop, hit memory pressure. SQLite began locking on concurrent writes to the execution table. Webhooks started timing out, the provider retried, and the retries added to the load. The container was OOM-killed and restarted — losing every in-flight execution, because they only existed in memory. Every element of that failure is addressed by the same set of changes: **Postgres instead of SQLite, queue mode instead of main mode, dedicated webhook processes, and workers you can scale horizontally.** This article is about running n8n like production infrastructure rather than a personal tool. ##### Production self-hosting fundamentals Three decisions distinguish a real deployment from a laptop demo. **Postgres, not SQLite.** SQLite is a single file with writer-level locking. It is fine for development and small single-user instances, and it becomes the bottleneck the moment you have concurrency or meaningful execution history. Migrate before you need to, because migrating a large SQLite database under pressure is unpleasant. **Configuration entirely through environment variables.** Nothing hard-coded, nothing configured only through the UI. This is what makes environments reproducible and upgrades safe. **Execution data pruning from day one.** n8n stores every execution's full data. At a few thousand executions a day with large payloads this grows to tens of gigabytes within weeks, and a bloated `execution_entity` table slows the whole instance. ```bash # The environment variables that matter most in production DB_TYPE=postgresdb DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST=postgres DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE=n8n DB_POSTGRESDB_USER=n8n DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD= DB_POSTGRESDB_POOL_SIZE=10 N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=<32+ random chars — BACK THIS UP SEPARATELY> N8N_HOST=automation.example.com N8N_PROTOCOL=https N8N_PORT=5678 WEBHOOK_URL=https://automation.example.com/ # must be the public URL GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata TZ=Asia/Kolkata # Housekeeping — prevents unbounded growth EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE=true EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE=168 # hours (7 days) EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE_MAX_COUNT=50000 EXECUTIONS_DATA_SAVE_ON_SUCCESS=all # 'none' saves a lot of space EXECUTIONS_DATA_SAVE_ON_ERROR=all N8N_LOG_LEVEL=info N8N_DIAGNOSTICS_ENABLED=false N8N_METRICS=true # Prometheus endpoint at /metrics ``` `WEBHOOK_URL` is a frequent source of confusion: it must be the externally reachable URL, because it is what n8n prints in the Webhook node. Behind a reverse proxy, the internal port and the public URL differ, and getting this wrong means the URLs you give providers do not work. ##### Main mode versus queue mode This is the central scaling concept and the assignment's main question. **Main mode** (the default) runs everything in one process: the editor UI, the REST API, webhook reception, schedule triggers, and workflow execution. Simple, and adequate up to perhaps a few thousand light executions per day. Its limits are structural — a single Node.js process has one event loop, so a CPU-heavy execution blocks others; memory is shared, so one large payload can OOM the whole instance; and scaling means a bigger machine, with a hard ceiling. **Queue mode** separates the roles. The **main** process serves the UI and API and *enqueues* executions rather than running them. **Worker** processes pull jobs from a **Redis** queue and execute them. Optional **webhook** processes handle only inbound HTTP, acknowledging fast without competing with executions. Why this enables horizontal scaling: workers are stateless and share nothing but Postgres and Redis. Adding capacity means starting more worker containers — on the same host or different hosts — with no reconfiguration. Throughput scales roughly linearly with worker count until the database becomes the constraint. A worker crash loses only its current job (which Redis re-queues), not the instance. ```mermaid flowchart TD I[Internet] --> LB[Reverse proxy
TLS termination] LB --> M[n8n MAIN
UI + API + schedulers] LB --> WH1[WEBHOOK process 1] LB --> WH2[WEBHOOK process 2] M -->|enqueue| R[(Redis
Bull queue)] WH1 -->|enqueue| R WH2 -->|enqueue| R R --> W1[WORKER 1
concurrency 10] R --> W2[WORKER 2
concurrency 10] R --> W3[WORKER 3
concurrency 10] M --- DB[(PostgreSQL
workflows, creds,
executions)] W1 --- DB W2 --- DB W3 --- DB ``` The Compose definition: ```yaml x-shared: &shared image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:1.80.0 # pin the version, never 'latest' restart: unless-stopped environment: &shared-env DB_TYPE: postgresdb DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST: postgres DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE: n8n DB_POSTGRESDB_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER} DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} EXECUTIONS_MODE: queue # the key setting QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST: redis QUEUE_HEALTH_CHECK_ACTIVE: "true" N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY: ${N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY} # IDENTICAL across all processes GENERIC_TIMEZONE: Asia/Kolkata TZ: Asia/Kolkata depends_on: postgres: { condition: service_healthy } redis: { condition: service_healthy } services: postgres: image: postgres:16-alpine restart: unless-stopped environment: POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER} POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} POSTGRES_DB: n8n volumes: [postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data] healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d n8n"] interval: 10s retries: 5 redis: image: redis:7-alpine restart: unless-stopped command: redis-server --appendonly yes volumes: [redis_data:/data] healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"] interval: 10s retries: 5 n8n-main: <<: *shared ports: ["5678:5678"] environment: <<: *shared-env N8N_HOST: ${N8N_HOST} N8N_PROTOCOL: https WEBHOOK_URL: https://${N8N_HOST}/ EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE: "true" EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE: "168" volumes: [n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n] n8n-worker: <<: *shared command: worker --concurrency=10 deploy: replicas: 3 # horizontal scaling knob n8n-webhook: <<: *shared command: webhook environment: <<: *shared-env WEBHOOK_URL: https://${N8N_HOST}/ volumes: { postgres_data: , redis_data: , n8n_data: } ``` Scale with `docker compose up -d --scale n8n-worker=6`. ##### Concurrency, and the encryption key **Worker concurrency** (`--concurrency=N`) sets how many executions one worker runs in parallel. Tuning depends on workload shape: I/O-bound workflows (mostly waiting on APIs) tolerate high concurrency — 10 to 20 per worker; CPU-bound work (large Code nodes, image or PDF processing) should stay near the CPU core count. Total parallelism is `workers × concurrency`, and the practical ceiling is usually Postgres connections: each worker holds a pool, so `workers × pool_size` must stay below your Postgres `max_connections`. **The encryption key** deserves its own emphasis, because losing it is unrecoverable. n8n encrypts every stored credential with `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. Three consequences: 1. **Every process must share the identical key.** A worker with a different key cannot decrypt credentials and every execution fails with confusing authentication errors. 2. **Losing the key means losing every credential permanently.** There is no recovery path — you re-enter all of them by hand. A database backup without the key is only half a backup. 3. **Back it up separately** from the database, in a password manager or secret manager. Storing it only in a `.env` file on the same server it protects defeats the purpose. If you never set it, n8n generates one and writes it to `~/.n8n/config` — which is exactly the file people forget to include in a volume, producing the classic "all my credentials broke after I recreated the container." ##### Backups, upgrades, and availability **Backups** cover three artefacts: the Postgres database (`pg_dump`, nightly, shipped offsite), the `.n8n` volume, and the encryption key (separately). Then prove a restore works in a scratch environment — an untested backup is a hypothesis. ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail STAMP=$(date +%F-%H%M) docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -Fc n8n \ > "/opt/backups/n8n-$STAMP.dump" rclone copy /opt/backups remote:n8n-backups find /opt/backups -type f -mtime +14 -delete ``` **Upgrades** on a clustered setup follow a fixed order, and getting it wrong causes schema mismatches: 1. Read the release notes for breaking changes. 2. Back up the database and verify the dump. 3. Test the new version in staging with a copy of production data. 4. Stop workers and webhook processes. 5. Upgrade and start **main** first — it runs the database migrations. 6. Wait for migrations to complete, then upgrade and start workers. 7. Verify with a smoke-test workflow. Always pin an explicit version tag. `latest` plus an unattended `docker compose pull` is how instances break at 3 a.m. **High availability** means removing single points of failure: multiple main instances behind a load balancer (with `N8N_MULTI_MAIN_SETUP_ENABLED=true` so schedule triggers do not double-fire), managed Postgres with replication, managed Redis, and health checks on `/healthz` driving automatic restarts. ##### Environments Separate dev, staging and production properly — distinct databases, distinct Redis, distinct credentials, distinct URLs. n8n's Source Control feature (Git-backed) lets you push workflows from dev to a repository and pull them into production, which turns workflow promotion into a reviewable pull request rather than a copy-paste. Where Source Control is unavailable, the disciplined fallback is exporting workflow JSON via the CLI (`n8n export:workflow --all --output=workflows.json`) into Git, with a documented import procedure. ##### Common pitfalls - **SQLite in production** — write locking under concurrency. - **Mismatched encryption keys** across processes, breaking all credentials. - **No key backup** — permanent credential loss. - **`latest` image tag**, causing surprise breaking upgrades. - **Workers upgraded before main**, hitting an un-migrated schema. - **No execution pruning** — the database grows until performance collapses. - **Wrong `WEBHOOK_URL`**, producing webhook URLs that nobody can reach. - **Postgres connection exhaustion** from `workers × pool_size` exceeding `max_connections`. - **Multiple main instances without multi-main enabled**, so every cron trigger fires twice. - **No `/healthz` monitoring**, so a wedged worker silently stops consuming. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: deploy n8n in **queue mode with Docker Compose** — main, Postgres, Redis and at least one worker — set the **encryption key via environment variables**, and run a workflow confirming a **worker, not main, executed it**. Verify by tailing worker logs (`docker compose logs -f n8n-worker`) while triggering the workflow; seeing the job appear in the worker's output rather than main's is the proof that queue mode is genuinely active. The mini project is a production-style cluster: **Postgres-backed, HTTPS, queue mode with multiple workers and a dedicated webhook process**, a **backup routine** for the database and encryption key, a **documented upgrade procedure**, and then a **load test** with concurrent executions. Use `hey` or `k6` to fire a few hundred concurrent webhooks and watch how the queue depth and worker utilization respond. Then scale workers from 1 to 3 and measure the throughput change — that measurement is the deliverable that demonstrates you understand horizontal scaling rather than merely configuring it. For the assignment, explain **main mode versus queue mode** and how queue mode enables horizontal scaling — stateless workers, shared Redis queue, linear throughput growth, isolated failures — and describe **why the encryption key must be preserved and backed up**, covering both the all-processes-must-match requirement and the unrecoverable-loss consequence. ##### Key takeaways - Production n8n means Postgres rather than SQLite, environment-variable configuration, pinned image versions, and execution pruning from day one. - Main mode runs everything in one event loop and scales only vertically; queue mode splits main, workers and webhook processes over a Redis queue. - Workers are stateless, so capacity scales horizontally by adding replicas — bounded in practice by Postgres connections (`workers × pool_size`). - The encryption key must be identical across every process and backed up separately from the database; losing it destroys all stored credentials irrecoverably. - Upgrade main first so migrations run before workers connect, back up and test restores, and monitor `/healthz` plus queue depth to catch wedged workers.
